plain_english: I believe — though my fellow Stoics wouldn't like to hear me say this — that Epicurus taught something good and pure. In fact, if you look closely, his teaching was quite strict. His famous idea about pleasure actually has very tight limits. He said pleasure should follow the same rule we Stoics say virtue should follow — obey nature. But luxury isn't satisfied with what nature actually needs.
original_excerpt: I myself believe, though my Stoic comrades would be unwilling to hear me say so, that the teaching of Epicurus was upright and holy, and even, if you examine it narrowly, stern: for this much talked of pleasure is reduced to a very narrow compass, and he bids pleasure submit to the same law which we bid virtue do—I mean, to obey nature. Luxury, however, is not satisfied with what is enough for nature.

plain_english: What happens then? Anyone who thinks happiness means lazy lounging around, stuffing yourself with food, and living wildly needs a good excuse for bad behavior. When he becomes an Epicurean — drawn in by that appealing school name — he doesn't follow the real pleasure they teach about. Instead, he follows the pleasure he already had in mind. Once he convinces himself that his bad habits match their philosophy, he stops being sneaky about his vices. He flaunts them openly in broad daylight.
original_excerpt: What is the consequence? Whoever thinks that happiness consists in lazy sloth, and alternations of gluttony and profligacy, requires a good patron for a bad action, and when he has become an Epicurean, having been led to do so by the attractive name of that school, he follows, not the pleasure which he there hears spoken of, but that which he brought thither with him, and, haying learned to think that his vices coincide with the maxims of that philosophy, he indulges in them no longer timidly and in dark corners, but boldly in the face of day.

plain_english: I won't follow most of my fellow Stoics and say that Epicurus teaches people to be criminals. But here's what I will say: his philosophy has a terrible reputation. And honestly? It doesn't deserve that reputation. "But how can you know this unless you've studied it deeply?" The problem is how it looks from the outside. It gives people an excuse to indulge their worst impulses. It's like seeing a brave soldier dressed in women's clothes. You know he's still honorable and strong underneath. Nothing shameful has actually happened to him. But there he is, holding a tambourine like some religious dancer.
original_excerpt: I will not, therefore, like most of our school, say that the sect of Epicurus is the teacher of crime, but what I say is: it is ill spoken of, it has a bad reputation, and yet it does not deserve it. "Who can know this without having been admitted to its inner mysteries?" Its very outside gives opportunity for scandal, and encourages men's baser desires: it is like a brave man dressed in a woman's gown: your chastity is assured, your manhood is safe, your body is submitted to nothing disgraceful, but your hand holds a drum (like a priest of Cybele).

plain_english: Choose a noble motto for your school of philosophy. Pick something that will inspire the mind. The sign over your door right now was created by vice itself. When someone sides with virtue, they show they have a noble character. But someone who chases pleasure looks weak, worn out, and degraded. They're destroying their own humanity and heading toward shameful vices — unless someone helps them sort out their pleasures. They need to learn which desires stay within natural limits and which ones are wild and endless. The crazy ones only get stronger the more you feed them.
original_excerpt: Choose, then, some honourable superscription for your school, some writing which shall in itself arouse the mind: that which at present stands over your door has been invented by the vices. He who ranges himself on the side of virtue gives thereby a proof of a noble disposition: he who follows pleasure appears to be weakly, worn out, degrading his manhood, likely to fall into infamous vices unless someone discriminates his pleasures for him, so that he may know which remain within the bounds of natural desire, which are frantic and boundless, and become all the more insatiable the more they are satisfied.

plain_english: But listen! Let virtue lead the way, and every step will be safe. Too much pleasure hurts us. But with virtue, we don't need to fear any kind of excess. Virtue naturally contains moderation within itself. Anything that gets damaged by having too much of it can't be truly good. And what better guide could there be than reason? After all, we're reasoning creatures. So if this combination appeals to you — if you want to reach a happy life this way — then let virtue lead. Let pleasure follow behind like a shadow hanging around the body. Only a mind incapable of great things would make virtue into pleasure's servant. Virtue is the highest quality we have.
original_excerpt: But come! let virtue lead the way: then every step will be safe. Too much pleasure is hurtful: but with virtue we need fear no excess of any kind, because moderation is contained in virtue herself. That which is injured by its own extent cannot be a good thing: besides, what better guide can there be than reason for beings endowed with a reasoning nature? so if this combination pleases you, if you are willing to proceed to a happy life thus accompanied, let virtue lead the way, let pleasure follow and hang about the body like a shadow: it is the part of a mind incapable of great things to hand over virtue, the highest of all qualities, as a handmaid to pleasure.
